violations.quote: Scale: text and pattern may each be several thousand characters long; recursion depth must not grow with their length, and each call must finish in about a second.
violations.judge_says: The last-star backtracking loop rescans all tokens after the star for each star position, giving quadratic behaviour on inputs such as thousands of 'a' characters matched against '*' followed by thousands of 'a's and a final 'b'.

violations.quote: Scale: text and pattern may each be several thousand characters long; recursion depth must not grow with their length, and each call must finish in about a second.
violations.judge_says: For a pattern containing many '[' characters with no closing ']', _tokenize calls _parse_class at each '[' and each call scans to the end of the pattern, giving quadratic parsing time.

violations.quote: Scale: text and pattern may each be several thousand characters long; recursion depth must not grow with their length, and each call must finish in about a second.
violations.judge_says: Its star backtracking rescans the token suffix for each star position (e.g. '*' followed by thousands of 'a's and a final 'b' against thousands of 'a's), and unclosed '[' classes are reparsed from each '['; both are quadratic in Python and can exceed about a second.

violations.quote: Scale: text and pattern may each be several thousand characters long; recursion depth must not grow with their length, and each call must finish in about a second.
violations.judge_says: For a pattern such as "*" followed by thousands of "a" characters and a final "b" against thousands of "a" characters, the code repeatedly rescans the long suffix after incrementing the star position, causing millions of Python-level loop iterations and likely exceeding about one second.

violations.quote: Scale: text and pattern may each be several thousand characters long; recursion depth must not grow with their length, and each call must finish in about a second.
violations.judge_says: When a class is unterminated, parse_class scans to the end of the pattern and the main loop then retries parsing from the next '[', giving O(pattern^2) work for patterns containing many unterminated '[' characters.

violations.quote: Scale: text and pattern may each be several thousand characters long; recursion depth must not grow with their length, and each call must finish in about a second.
violations.judge_says: The last-star backtracking matcher rescans the token suffix after each star extension, giving O(len(text) * len(tokens)) worst-case work with a Python function call per character for adversarial patterns such as many '*a' items followed by a failing literal.

violations.quote: Scale: text and pattern may each be several thousand characters long; recursion depth must not grow with their length, and each call must finish in about a second.
violations.judge_says: On a mismatch the iterative matcher backs up to the last '*' and rescans the following tokens for each advanced text position, giving O(len(text) * len(pattern)) Python-level steps (e.g. '*' + many 'a's + 'b' against many 'a's) that can exceed about a second.

violations.quote: Scale: text and pattern may each be several thousand characters long; recursion depth must not grow with their length, and each call must finish in about a second.
violations.judge_says: An unterminated '[' is tentatively scanned to the end of the pattern and then reparsed starting one character later, so patterns containing many unterminated '[' characters cause O(len(pattern)^2) tokenization work.

violations.quote: After reading a member x, if the next character is "-" and the character after that exists and is not "]", then a second member y is read the same way and the pair is the range of all characters from x to y inclusive (by code point).
violations.judge_says: In _parse_class the very-first ']' member is appended as an isolated interval and bypasses the range check, so e.g. "[]-a]" is treated as members ']', '-', 'a' instead of the range ']'-'a', wrongly matching '-' and missing characters like '`'.

violations.quote: Scale: text and pattern may each be several thousand characters long; recursion depth must not grow with their length, and each call must finish in about a second.
violations.judge_says: The matcher backtracks by incrementing star_si and re-scanning all tokens after the last '*' each time, giving O(len(text) * len(tokens)) behaviour (e.g. text 'a'*3000 vs pattern '*' + 'a'*2999 + 'b') that can exceed about a second in Python for several-thousand-character inputs.

violations.quote: round the value to one decimal place (it is never exactly halfway)
violations.judge_says: The code rounds up only when 2 * r > u, so 1792 bytes (exactly 1.75 KiB) is formatted as "1.7 KiB" instead of rounding up to "1.8 KiB".

probes.note: 1792 B = 1.75 KiB and 2304 B = 2.25 KiB are exact ties, which the docstring says never occur (the human_size spec defect); the reference rounds half to even.

violations.quote: divide n by u and round the value to one decimal place (it is never exactly halfway)
violations.judge_says: It uses `if 2 * r > u` so an exact half (e.g. 1792 bytes = 1.75 KiB, where 2*r == u) rounds down to "1.7 KiB" instead of up to "1.8 KiB".

probes.note: 1792 B = 1.75 KiB and 2304 B = 2.25 KiB are exact ties, which the docstring says never occur (the human_size spec defect); the reference rounds half to even.

violations.quote: 1. TypeError if start or end is not a date, or is a datetime.
violations.judge_says: Using `type(start) is not date` also rejects non-datetime subclasses of date, which are dates and are not datetimes.

violations.quote: 2. TypeError if weekday or n is not an int, or is a bool.
violations.judge_says: Using `type(weekday) is not int` also rejects non-bool subclasses of int, which are ints and are not bools.

violations.quote: TypeError if start or end is not a date, or is a datetime.
violations.judge_says: It uses `type(start) is not datetime.date`, rejecting non-datetime subclasses of date even though they are dates and only datetime is excluded.

violations.quote: TypeError if weekday or n is not an int, or is a bool.
violations.judge_says: It uses `type(weekday) is not int or type(n) is not int`, rejecting non-bool int subclasses even though only bool is specifically excluded.

violations.quote: TypeError if start or end is not a date, or is a datetime.
violations.judge_says: It uses `type(start) is not date or type(end) is not date`, so a non-datetime subclass of `datetime.date` incorrectly raises TypeError instead of being accepted.

violations.quote: TypeError if weekday or n is not an int, or is a bool.
violations.judge_says: It uses `type(weekday) is not int or type(n) is not int`, so a non-bool subclass of `int` incorrectly raises TypeError instead of being accepted.

violations.quote: "MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH" or "MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH-PRERELEASE", with nothing else: no surrounding whitespace, no "v" prefix, no "+build" suffix.
violations.judge_says: Because the numeric and identifier regexes use `$` (which matches before a final newline) rather than a strict full match, versions such as "1.0.0\n" or "1.0.0-alpha\n" are accepted instead of raising ValueError.

violations.quote: capacity: the maximum number of tokens, an int or float, finite and > 0.
violations.judge_says: It calls math.isfinite on the raw int, which raises OverflowError for finite ints too large to convert to float such as 10**400 instead of accepting them (the same flaw affects rate, timestamps, and costs).

violations.quote: capacity: the maximum number of tokens, an int or float, finite and > 0.
violations.judge_says: It calls math.isfinite(capacity), which raises OverflowError for a finite int too large to convert to float (e.g. 10**400) instead of accepting it; the same math.isfinite flaw applies to large-int rate, timestamp, and cost values.

violations.quote: capacity: the maximum number of tokens, an int or float, finite and > 0.
violations.judge_says: It calls math.isfinite on the raw value, so a finite huge int such as 10**400 raises OverflowError instead of being accepted (the same flaw affects rate, timestamp, and cost).

violations.quote: capacity: the maximum number of tokens, an int or float, finite and > 0.
violations.judge_says: It calls math.isfinite() directly on ints, so a valid huge int such as 10**400 raises OverflowError during conversion to float instead of being accepted as finite, and the same issue affects large rate, timestamp, and cost values.

violations.quote: capacity: the maximum number of tokens, an int or float, finite and > 0.
violations.judge_says: It calls math.isfinite(capacity) (and similarly for rate, timestamps and costs), which raises OverflowError for a huge int such as 10**400 instead of accepting it as a finite positive int.

violations.quote: capacity: the maximum number of tokens, an int or float, finite and > 0.
violations.judge_says: It calls math.isfinite() on every numeric input, which raises OverflowError for valid huge ints such as 10**400 instead of treating them as finite and proceeding (the same flaw applies to rate, timestamp, and cost).

violations.quote: capacity: the maximum number of tokens, an int or float, finite and > 0.
violations.judge_says: It calls math.isfinite(capacity), which raises OverflowError for a valid int larger than about 1e308 instead of accepting it as finite.

violations.quote: rate: tokens added per second, an int or float, finite and >= 0.
violations.judge_says: It calls math.isfinite(rate), which raises OverflowError for a valid int larger than about 1e308 instead of accepting it as finite.

violations.quote: timestamp (seconds) is an int or float, finite, and not less than the previous request's timestamp. cost is an int or float, finite and > 0.
violations.judge_says: It calls math.isfinite on timestamp and cost, so valid ints larger than about 1e308 raise OverflowError instead of being processed.

violations.quote: capacity: the maximum number of tokens, an int or float, finite and > 0.
violations.judge_says: It calls math.isfinite() directly on int inputs, so a huge finite int such as 10**400 raises OverflowError instead of being accepted (the same flaw applies to rate, timestamp, and cost).

violations.quote: For n > 0, step forward one day at a time from start and count each business day; the result is the n-th business day counted.
violations.judge_says: After skipping or processing a bulk week it continues with cur on a Monday but the loop head counts only days strictly after cur, so that Monday is never counted; e.g. from 2026-01-05 with a later holiday present, n=10 is returned as 2026-01-20 instead of 2026-01-19.

violations.quote: For n < 0, do the same backwards and return the |n|-th business day counted. start itself is never counted, and it need not be a business day.
violations.judge_says: Symmetrically, after moving cur to a Friday it re-enters the loop head which counts only days before cur, so that Friday is never counted; e.g. business_days(date(2026,1,16), -10, {date(2026,1,1)}) returns 2025-12-31 instead of 2026-01-02.
